newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to sell $38 billion of securities next week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to sell $38 billion of securities next week.

text.p: With the budget deficit falling, the Treasury Department announced Wednesday that it will bring another $38 billion of debt securities to market next week.

The Treasury will sell $16 billion in three-year notes Tuesday, $12 billion in 10-year notes next Wednesday and $10 billion of 30-year bonds next Thursday as part of its continuing borrowing activity to pay off older goverment debt and to pay for government spending programmes.
Despite widespread speculation that the Treasury might be able to eliminate some issues because of the sharply tumbling budget deficit, there was no indication of any plan to do so.
Deputy Assistant Treasury Secretary Roger Anderson, responding to questions at a news conference, said the Treasury was not considering dropping any issues.
"We are not currently contemplating any further cycle changes," Anderson said.

Many analysts think the government's budget deficit for the fiscal year ending Sept. 30 will be under $50 billion, a major improvement from a year ago when the Clinton administration was forecasting a shortfall of $125 billion.

The main reason for the decline has been a flood of tax revenues from economic growth and from a booming stock market. Higher revenues from taxes means the Treasury needs to borrow less to finance government spending.

Any changes in Treasury borrowing could ripple through financial markets since rates paid on Treasury securities are used as a benchmark for home mortgages, corporate loans and a host of other loan rates. But fewer Treasury securities could make the market less liquid and less useful as a yardstick for setting other rates.
A private-sector Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee recommended to the Treasury that it would be better to reduce the size of future offerings rather than to eliminate some maturities altogether.

The panel, however, warned there were "practical limitations" to how far the weekly bill offerings could be reduced without hurting the market's liquidity. But it added that this was not a "current concern" given recent increases in the weekly bill auctions.
Kevin Harris, an economist with MCM MoneyWatch in New York, said next week's auctions were about as expected by market participants and had little impact on bond prices Tuesday.
The bellwether 30-year Treasury rose 26/32, or $8.13 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.33 percent, the lowest since Feb. 16, 1996.

The Treasury said next week's auctions will pay off $26.8 billion of maturing securities and raise $11.2 billion of new cash for financing government operations during the July-September third quarter.
